title: Periphery sandwiched between two array wafers, bitline pairs across bonds
idea: Reverse the CMOS-under-array order: thin the periphery wafer and hybrid-bond array wafers to BOTH faces (one face-down above, one face-up below). Each sense amplifier takes its true bitline from the upper array and its complement/reference bitline from the lower array, so one SA stripe and one decoder set serve two arrays.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die (fact 7): periphery silicon per bit halves (~1.6-1.8x bits per periphery-wafer area); arrays get unrestricted thermal budget; mirrored open-bitline pairs see matched noise.

title: Flip the wafer: etch storage capacitors from the backside
idea: Build access transistors and bitlines on the front, bond to a carrier, thin the silicon to ~2-3 um, then etch capacitor holes from the backside landing directly on each storage-node junction and fill with MIM. Capacitor height is set by backside film thickness instead of fighting front-side BEOL, and bitline contacts no longer weave between capacitor pillars.
why: Capacitor wall + 6F2 congestion (facts 1,4): removing storage-node contacts/landing pads from the front frees ~20-30% of cell area toward 4F2 and lets capacitor height grow independently of bitline routing.

title: Rotate alternate 3D tiers 90 degrees to split staircases
idea: In a lateral 3D DRAM stack, rotate every other tier's cell orientation 90 degrees so odd-tier bitlines run X and even-tier bitlines run Y. Odd tiers stair-step on the east/west edges and even tiers on north/south, so each staircase is half as tall, and vertically adjacent bitlines only cross at points instead of running parallel.
why: 3D blockers (fact 2): staircase footprint per edge halves (~20-30% array-efficiency gain at 64+ tiers) and inter-tier bitline coupling drops ~5-10x, allowing thinner tiers.

title: Reverse the plate's role: drop the plate to park idle cells
idea: Segment the capacitor plate per subarray and, when a subarray goes idle, ramp its plate down ~0.3-0.4 V so all floating storage nodes couple down with it; stored '1's then sit at lower field versus the gate/junction (less GIDL and trap-assisted leakage) while '0's sit slightly below ground held off by the negative back-bias. The plate ramps back up before the next activation, restoring the levels.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): GIDL/TAT leakage is exponential in field, so a 0.3-0.4 V reduction could cut tail leakage 3-10x, stretching refresh intervals and cutting the 16-33% idle refresh power proportionally.

title: Sense amps flipped beneath array, one per 128-cell bitline
idea: Move sense amplifiers from mat edges to a logic wafer hybrid-bonded underneath, with one ~0.4 um-pitch bond per 128-cell bitline segment (staggered so pads fit), giving every short bitline its own SA directly below. Bitline capacitance falls ~6-8x versus 1k-cell bitlines, so a ~1 fF capacitor delivers today's signal.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): capacitor AR can fall from 60-75:1 to ~10-15:1, removing the hardest etch; shorter bitlines also cut sensing energy and latency.

title: Pattern first, stack later: DUV tiers bonded into 3D
idea: Reverse 3D's 'stack then pattern through all tiers': each tier is a complete relaxed-pitch (F~35 nm, DUV-only) 2D DRAM-lite layer built on its own donor wafer, tested, then ion-cut transferred onto the stack with a coarse inter-tier via; repeat 8-16 times. Density comes from tier count, not EUV pitch.
why: Litho/capital (fact 4): zero EUV layers; 16 tiers at ~1/8 the density per tier still give ~2x 2D density, using depreciated DUV fabs and known-good-tier yield control.

title: Vertical capacitor column segmented per tier, lateral transistors
idea: Swap the usual 3D orientation: keep transistors lateral in each tier but etch one deep vertical capacitor trench per cell column through all tiers; each tier's storage-node layer is exposed as a ring on the trench wall (isolated from neighbors by the inter-tier dielectric), a scalloped recess enlarges it, then one conformal high-k and a common plate fill finish every tier's capacitor at once.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): one HAR etch makes N tiers of ~0.7-1.5 fF capacitors without lateral capacitor recess; viable with short bitlines, aiming at break-even below 26 tiers.

title: Stand DRAM dies on edge: TSV-free sideways HBM
idea: Rotate the HBM stack 90 degrees: bond thin core dies into a block, saw and polish one face so every die's edge exposes its top-metal lines, then hybrid-bond that polished edge face directly onto the logic die. Each die talks through thousands of edge wires along its 10 mm edge instead of TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV keep-out area and TSV yield loss; 1-2 um edge pitch gives 5,000-10,000 lines per die; heat conducts along die planes into the base.

title: Capacitor first, vertical transistor regrown over it, bitline on top
idea: Reverse the 4F2 vertical-channel order: etch and fill storage capacitor trenches first in bulk silicon (annealed at ~1000 C for crystalline high-k), cap them, grow silicon laterally over them by epitaxial lateral overgrowth, form the vertical-channel transistor in the regrown silicon, and put the bitline on top. The notoriously hard buried bitline of 4F2 VCT disappears.
why: Density + capacitor wall (facts 1,4): 4F2 (+33% cells/area vs 6F2) with a capacitor not limited by BEOL height and a high-temperature dielectric (k~40+).

title: Make the interposer the memory: DRAM-filled active interposer
idea: Swap substrate and memory roles: build the large silicon interposer under an accelerator (2,500+ mm2, relaxed 40-65 nm pitch, mostly empty silicon) as an 8-tier relaxed-pitch DRAM array with routing on top, so the accelerator sits directly on ~100 GB of memory with micron-scale vertical access.
why: Data movement and HBM tax (facts 5,6): turns wasted interposer area into memory at <1 pJ/bit, no TSV stack, made in mature-node fabs including U.S. ones.

title: Rotate the page vertical: one cell per tier, 64-bit activation
idea: In 3D DRAM, reverse the activation axis: a short vertical word-pillar gates exactly one cell in each of 64 tiers, and each tier senses on its own horizontal bitline, so one activation opens a 64-bit vertical column instead of an 8 kb row.
why: Overfetch and row hammer (facts 8,9): activation energy per useful bit drops ~50-100x; an aggressor pillar disturbs only its few neighbors, not a whole row.

title: Split the cell across wafers: capacitors bonded onto transistors
idea: Fabricate storage capacitors on a separate wafer where perovskite (Ba,Sr)TiO3 can be crystallized at 650-750 C (k~100-300), then bond it face-to-face onto the transistor wafer through a self-aligning nano-pad lattice and strip the capacitor carrier. Transistor and capacitor never share a thermal budget.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): k>100 means AR <20 for 5 fF, removing the AR-115 requirement; the real risk is ~50 nm-pitch bonding versus today's ~400 nm.

title: Bitlines on the backside, wordlines on the front
idea: Rearrange the routing planes: after front-side transistor and capacitor formation, flip and thin the wafer and form bitlines on the backside contacting the bottom of each vertical channel, so bitlines and capacitors never compete for the same front-side layers.
why: Layout congestion and signal margin (facts 1,4): bitlines become wide low-R lines with air gaps (~30% less bitline capacitance = proportionally smaller Cs) and the front side can pack capacitors at 4F2.

title: Sell tiers, not dies: overbuild tiers, fuse bad ones out
idea: Build early 3D DRAM with deliberately overprovisioned tiers (e.g. 40 built, 32 sold), test each tier through its own staircase contact, and map defective tiers out with tier-level fuses. This reverses the yield model from 'one defect kills the die' to 'a defect costs one tier'.
why: 3D break-even (fact 2): lifting die yield from ~40% to >90% for immature processes at 25% extra tier cost cuts cost per good bit ~45%, pulling 3D in years earlier.

title: Charge-coupled pillar: vertical shift-register DRAM, no capacitor
idea: Reverse 3D NAND's vertical string: store charge packets under each word-tier gate of an oxide-semiconductor channel pillar and clock them up the pillar CCD-style (three-phase gates) to one sense node at the top, so each pillar is a 64-bit vertical shift register with no per-bit transistor or capacitor.
why: Capacitor wall and 3D cell (facts 1,2): bit = one gate tier x pillar pitch on a 3D NAND-like line; IGZO's low leakage gives ms retention; ~1 ns/stage keeps a 64-bit block read under ~100 ns; charge has unlimited endurance.

title: Capacitor that switches itself: Mott-selector-in-capacitor crosspoint
idea: Fold the transistor's role into the capacitor stack: metal / high-k / NbO2 Mott threshold layer / metal, where the Mott layer snaps conductive above ~1 V to charge the cell and returns insulating below, forming a transistor-free 1S1C crosspoint that can be stacked in BEOL.
why: 4F2 crosspoint stacking (facts 2,4); honest catch: selector off-current must fall below ~1e-17 A for ms retention, so first use is a us-retention refresh-heavy cache tier.

title: Counter-phase wordline drive on adjacent tiers cancels coupling
idea: In stacked 3D DRAM, whenever a tier's selected wordline ramps up, drive an unselected wordline segment in each neighboring tier down by a matched step (deeper off-state), so vertical capacitive kicks into the neighbors' bitlines and storage nodes cancel instead of accumulating.
why: Inter-tier disturb and row hammer (facts 2,9): 2-4x less vertical coupling lets tier pitch shrink (more tiers per um of stack) and lowers disturb-driven refresh.

title: Twist vertical bitline pairs mid-stack for folded-pair noise cancellation
idea: Pair adjacent vertical bitline pillars as true/complement and swap their positions halfway up the stack through a crossover in a middle tier, so each sees equal coupling from every neighbor and the bottom sense amp gets a common-mode-free differential signal, restoring folded-bitline immunity in 3D.
why: Sense margin in 3D/open-bitline arrays (facts 1,2): 30-50% more usable margin allows ~30% smaller Cs or longer bitlines.

title: Invert the supply chain: U.S. makes periphery, bonds arrays
idea: Use the CMOS-bonded-array split to reverse where value sits: periphery wafers come from existing U.S. 28-40 nm logic fabs, array-only wafers come from a lean new U.S. array fab or allied DRAM fabs, and hybrid bonding plus test happen domestically.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4): an array-only fab skips ~40% of process steps; underused U.S. mature-node fabs supply periphery; capacity in ~2 years versus 5.

title: Lay the capacitor flat and laminate it: MLCC-in-cell
idea: Replace the tall cylinder with a nanoscale multilayer ceramic capacitor: 6-10 alternating TiN/ZrO2 layers ALD-deposited laterally into a recess, with even electrodes tied to the storage node at one sidewall and odd ones to the plate at the other via selective alternating recess. Capacitance scales with layer count, not aspect ratio.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and lateral 3D tiers (fact 2): ~5 fF in a short footprint with no litho for added capacitance, only ALD cycles.

title: Sense amps built from tier transistors inside each 3D tier
idea: Swap periphery and array roles in an oxide-semiconductor 3D DRAM: build n-only clocked, capacitively bootstrapped sense amplifiers from the same IGZO transistors beside every mat in every tier, so each tier senses locally and only digital data drops to the CMOS base.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and 3D bitline routing (fact 2): removes the vertical analog bitline-to-CMOS bottleneck and keeps bitlines short per tier; ~5-10 ns slower sensing is tolerable.

title: Pillars first, tiers grown around them
idea: Invert stack-then-etch: start with short vertical Mo bitline pillar stubs on the base, then build each tier bottom-up around them (deposit and planarize dielectric and channel), extending each pillar by area-selective deposition per tier, so no 60+ tier high-aspect-ratio hole etch is ever needed.
why: 3D process wall (fact 2): removes the HAR etch and its hardmask cost; tier count is limited by deposition cycles rather than etch AR.

title: Face-to-face HBM pairs halve the TSV count
idea: Rearrange HBM from face-to-back stacking to face-to-face pairs: two core dies are hybrid-bonded face-to-face at ~1 um pitch with no TSVs between them, and only pair-to-pair interfaces use TSVs, with one die's TSVs serving both.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV count and keep-out area halve; dense face-to-face bonds let two dies share I/O and repair logic; ~10-15% more bits per wafer and better stack yield.

title: Two-deck capacitor reusing one hole mask for AR 120
idea: Reverse 'one tall etch' into 'stack, etch, stack, etch': etch and line deck-1 capacitor holes, deposit a second mold deck, and re-expose the SAME capacitor mask aligned to deck 1 so deck-2 holes land on deck-1 electrodes, forming one continuous electrode. Zero new masks: one existing mask is used twice.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): reaches the AR ~115-120 needed for more charge using two AR-60 etches already in production, for ~1.6-1.8x Cs or a shrunken footprint.

title: Capacitor first, IGZO transistor last, perovskite dielectric
idea: Re-sequence the flow: build the capacitor array first in the silicon wafer and crystallize a SrTiO3 dielectric (k~100+) at 700 C, then build low-temperature (<400 C) IGZO vertical access transistors on top by re-using the existing active/wordline/bitline masks; the only added mask is the via from capacitor top to transistor drain.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and leakage tail (fact 3): reaches k~100 with no 1000 C anneal hitting the transistor; IGZO off-current (<1e-19 A/um) shrinks the leakage tail.

title: One grayscale mask cuts every 3D tier contact
idea: Replace the multi-mask trim-etch staircase with a single grayscale reticle whose resist-thickness steps transfer through a proportional etch, opening contacts to all 64 tiers at graded depths in one exposure: a reversed staircase made of holes instead of terraces.
why: 3D cost (fact 2): staircase masks drop from ~4-8 to 1 and staircase area shrinks ~3x, moving break-even toward fewer tiers.

title: One line mask, rotated 90 degrees, makes 4F2 crosspoints
idea: Use a single SAQP mandrel mask twice: expose it, then rotate the wafer 90 degrees and expose it again on a second hardmask, so its lines define both the wordline and bitline grids and their intersections self-align the vertical-channel pillars of a 4F2 cell.
why: Litho/EUV (fact 4) and density: 4F2 (+33% bits/area) with one shared critical mask instead of two, and perfect pitch match between wordline and bitline grids.

title: One wordline-cut mask halves every page
idea: Add one cut mask that splits each wordline at mat center, and re-wire the existing interleaved sub-wordline drivers (even rows driven from the left, odd from the right) so each half-wordline is driven from its own side, letting the controller open half-pages independently.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): activation energy and row-hammer exposure per access halve, for a small sub-wordline-driver area cost and one mask.

title: Inside-out flower cell: plate in the hole, transistors radiating
idea: Invert the lateral 3D DRAM cell: each through-stack hole holds a shared plate pillar; the tier's silicon around it is recessed into a ring capacitor, and 4-6 lateral access transistors radiate outward to per-tier horizontal bitlines. Built on a 3D NAND tool line reusing its hole and slit mask types, plus one added plate-contact mask.
why: 3D cell (fact 2) and capacitor (fact 1): each hole serves 4-6 cells per tier with capacitor area growing with hole circumference, roughly doubling bits per hole versus one-cell-per-hole lateral designs.

title: Recess only passing-wordline segments with one mask
idea: Rearrange the buried wordline: one added mask exposes only the segments where wordlines cross isolation (the passing gates) and recesses them deeper, moving their field away from the neighboring cell's storage junction while active-crossing segments stay at normal depth.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): passing-gate coupling drives the ~1k-activation threshold; a deeper passing segment could raise it several-fold with zero cell-area cost.

title: Capacitor holes extended into nano-TSVs inside the array
idea: Repurpose the capacitor lattice: in HBM core dies thinned to ~3 um, one added mask selects every 64th capacitor site for an extended etch through to the backside, turning those holes into ~30 nm nano-TSVs spread through the array instead of large TSVs in dedicated keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes most TSV keep-out area and gives thousands of vertical links per mat, a large step toward DDR5-like area per bit for HBM.

title: Reverse-graded threshold tiers replace the 3D staircase
idea: Each tier gets two series n-type select transistors whose thresholds are graded in opposite directions across the stack (set by deposition recipe per tier, no mask). Driving pillar A to Vt_j+d and pillar B to Vt'_j+d leaves only tier j with both transistors conducting: a window decoder. The only added mask is the two select-pillar holes.
why: 3D cost and area (fact 2): replaces most of the staircase with ~16-20 voltage-decoded tiers per coarse group, cutting staircase masks and area by ~10x.

title: One via mask personalizes page, bank and 2T2C mode
idea: Business model reversal: fabricate a single universal DRAM wafer and make products with one via mask that rewires mats into 1 kB or 2 kB pages, HBM pseudo-channels, or a 2T2C mode (two cells per bit for double signal and ~10x retention, half density) for automotive and low-refresh customers.
why: Capital (fact 4) and supply flexibility: one wafer flow serves many SKUs; capacity shifts between markets within weeks; the 2T2C SKU attacks refresh (fact 3).

title: Rotate the crystal under the layout for quieter channels
idea: Zero added masks: rotate the 4F2 vertical-channel array 45 degrees relative to the wafer notch (or start from (110) wafers) so channel sidewalls become {100} planes, which have ~3x lower interface-trap density than {110}.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): the trap-assisted tail sets refresh, so fewer interface traps can shift the ~13 fA tail down and stretch refresh intervals for the price of a layout rotation.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina grows the capacitor mold
idea: Reverse etching a mold into growing one: deposit ~2 um of aluminum over the landing pads, use one added mask to imprint pore nucleation dimples aligned to the pads, and anodize so self-ordered pores grow straight down at AR >100; line the pores with TiN/high-k/TiN.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): AR 100-150 with no plasma HAR etch and no support-lattice masks; AAO pore AR >1000 is proven at larger pitch.

title: Glass-panel DRAM self-aligned by backside exposure
idea: Build oxide-semiconductor DRAM tiers on large glass panels and expose the photoresist through the glass from below, so the opaque buried wordlines act as the mask for the channel/source-drain pattern above them; the only added mask is the panel contact opening.
why: Capital and litho (fact 4): panel area is ~10x a 300 mm wafer, display fabs have spare capacity, and self-alignment removes a critical overlay step.

title: Castellated kerf vias: TSVs moved to die edges
idea: Move vertical interconnect from die interior to edge: one added mask etches via trenches in the dicing streets, and sawing through their centers leaves half-vias on each die's sidewall. After stacking, the aligned sidewall half-vias are connected vertically by plating or printed redistribution.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): frees interior TSV keep-out area for cells and avoids TSV-induced stress and yield loss.

title: Mirror tier pairs to share bitline layers
idea: Flip every second tier upside down so tiers 2k and 2k+1 face each other and share one bitline/contact layer between them (the 3D NAND mirror trick applied to 3D DRAM). It is done by deposition order alone, with zero added masks.
why: Stack height and 3D cost (fact 2): ~25-30% fewer layers per bit tier means more tiers within the same HAR etch budget.

title: Back-plane under each tier becomes a retention lock
idea: Reverse the gate side: each IGZO tier sits on a blanket conductive back-plane, held at 0 V during access and pulsed to about -1 V when the subarray idles, pushing the channel deep into depletion. The only added mask is the back-plane contact.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): decades lower off-current during idle, potentially second-scale retention and near-zero refresh power in standby.

title: Public golden DRAM array mask set, one private mask
idea: Policy: fund an open, government-owned reference DRAM array mask set and process (the cell, capacitor and bitline layers) that any U.S. fab or startup can license, each differentiating with one private periphery or personalization mask, reversing DRAM from closed IP to shared infrastructure.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability (fact 4): removes the multi-year array development barrier for new entrants; mask NRE is shared across all fabs.

title: Roll a 2D array film into a multi-turn scroll
idea: Turn area into tiers by rolling instead of stacking: fabricate a thin-film oxide DRAM array on a strained bilayer membrane with the existing mask set, then use one added release mask so the film self-rolls into a 10-30 turn Swiss roll, with turns connected through contacts at the scroll edge.
why: Density and 3D cost (facts 2,4): 10-30x bits per footprint without per-tier processing; rolled-up nanomembrane capacitors already exist.

title: Maskless interference lithography for the array, one trim mask
idea: Reverse which part needs a mask: pattern the periodic capacitor lattice with three-beam 193 nm interference (no reticle) at ~70 nm pitch, multiply hole density with block-copolymer DSA, and add one cheap DUV trim mask that blocks the lattice outside the arrays.
why: EUV dependence and capital (fact 4): removes an EUV layer from the 5-7 per wafer, cutting critical-layer cost by roughly 3-5x.

title: Inductive coupling coils replace HBM signal TSVs
idea: Swap the wire for a field: core dies talk vertically through on-chip coil pairs drawn in existing top metal (zero masks), and power rides highly doped silicon vias made with the one added implant mask, so the HBM stack needs no metal TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV keep-out, no Cu-TSV stress or yield loss; coil links reach ~1 pJ/bit at tens of um vertical spacing.

title: NMOS-only sub-wordline drivers bootstrapped by cell capacitors
idea: Rearrange the sub-wordline driver: drop the PMOS and its N-well spacing and revive 1970s NMOS bootstrap drivers, using array-process cylinder capacitors as bootstrap capacitors so wordlines still reach ~3 V. Zero added masks: it is a layout change.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die (fact 7): sub-wordline driver stripes shrink ~30-40% (well spacing dominates them), giving roughly 3-5% more bits per die.

title: Tungsten-free TiN wordlines stitched to Cu every 128 cells
idea: Reverse the wordline's job: buried TiN-only lines just gate the cells, while a copper strap above carries the current, connected every 128 cells through one added stitch-contact mask. RC falls ~16x, which covers TiN's ~4x higher resistivity.
why: Scarce resources (China ~80% of tungsten): removes tungsten from the array's largest use; U.S. supply resilience.

title: Rotate alternate mats 90 degrees for transposed access
idea: Rotate every second mat 90 degrees in layout (zero added masks), so data written row-major lands column-major there; the controller reads a matrix row from normal mats or its transpose from rotated mats with a single activation.
why: Data movement (fact 5): AI transposes (attention K^T, gradients) no longer move through caches, saving a read/write round trip of ~10-20 pJ/bit per transposed byte.
